summary:
On Mars, dust steals the power and radiation limits the time to fix it.

KŌMAKU: Dust & Radiation is a Mars mission-control game for ages 7–12 by Team Roshan Xingbo. It is a game where kids step into that real conflict, a new angle on space science.

We turn complex space science into fun stories young astronauts can understand.

Through an outpost window, players guide their teammate’s solar-panel cleaning, watch dust clear and energy collect, and explore radiation exposure during a fictional storm countdown. Short, replayable missions connect their decisions to simple equations.

NASA’s Curiosity radiation measurements, Pathfinder dust research, and rover power studies ground the learning. Measured evidence is clearly distinguished from game settings.

Our contribution to the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge is bringing dust and radiation into one understandable experience. 

Players practice predicting, monitoring resources, comparing strategies, and explaining cause and effect. 

The goal is to help children understand how scientific decisions work in a fresh new scientifically educational angle—not simply memorize facts. Learning gains still need evaluation with children and educators.

In the future version, we want to introduce an adaptive system with new astronauts with different strengths, limited resources, and changing missions.

 A junor astronaut playing KŌMAKU would hopefully be a true explorer on Mars in the future.
details:
On Mars, dust steals the power and radiation limits the time to fix it.

KŌMAKU: Dust & Radiation puts children inside mission control, looking through an outpost window at their teammate, Ren, cleaning a dusty solar panel. The player chooses her cleaning pace, watches the panel clear, and sees how solar generation changes the habitat’s stored energy. A fictional radiation-storm countdown introduces the importance of time and exposure.

We turn scientists’ complex space knowledge into fun stories young astronauts can understand in a fresh new angle on radiation and dust.

How the experience works

A story introduces the mission. Science explanations introduce the concepts behind the task, and the playable round lasts about 90 active seconds. Players change the cleaning pace and observe the consequences. A simplified fatigue model means requesting the fastest pace does not always produce the most effective work.

The result connects the mission to understandable relationships:

  • Cleaning removes dust, allowing more sunlight to reach the panel.
  • Solar generation supplies the habitat; generation minus consumption changes stored battery energy.
  • Radiation dose accumulates from dose rate over time.
  • Requested pace and effective cleaning rate can differ because of the game’s fatigue model.

Players can pause to explore explanations and replay to compare strategies. The current development version also includes contextual coaching and a local journal of recent attempts. These records show activity and results, rather than claiming to measure mastery.

What makes it different

Our contribution is an integrated learning experience: NASA dust, radiation, and rover-power research meet in one understandable task. Children can see why a cleaner panel changes power, and why power, stored energy, and radiation dose are different quantities. Replay makes ideas testable.

The novelty is the teaching design and connected feedback, with a new angle on connecting radiation and dust on Mars. We are connecting the above-mentioned established scientific elements and concepts through gameplay—not claiming a newly discovered physical relationship between dust and radiation.

The visual experience combines a Mars outpost, an animated teammate, visible panel cleaning, and Asian-inspired design. The player participates in a story while investigating the systems behind it.

How NASA resources make it possible

Curiosity’s Radiation Assessment Detector provides a historical Mars surface reference of approximately 210 ± 40 microgray per Earth day, measured in its tissue-like detector. Pathfinder research provides evidence that settled dust reduces solar-cell output. Mars Exploration Rover power research informs the distinction between generating power, consuming power, and storing energy.

An optional NASA Solar Dynamics Observatory viewer displays the latest available solar image, with availability and cache information. This is an observation of the Sun, not a live Mars radiation reading or the source of our storm countdown.

Our cleaning rates, fatigue, storm timing, equipment specifications, and scoring thresholds are authored teaching settings. In the current mission, cleaning pace changes cleaning and energy outcomes; all completed rounds share the same outside duration and accumulated model dose. We do not present the simulation as a medical risk assessment or flight-certified training.

Skills and intended impact

The game provides opportunities to practice prediction, monitoring, resource management, comparison, and scientific explanation. Children can investigate questions such as: Did my plan clear more dust? Did that produce more energy? Why is power different from stored energy?

Offline play and short rounds make repeated practice possible without a learner account. Our next evaluation step is testing with children and educators, using predictions, explanations, and later recall to assess understanding.

How we built it

The game uses the open-source Godot engine and GDScript, with Python supporting build tools, validation, and scientific documentation. The simulation is separated from the visuals and interface so changes to the presentation do not silently change the equations. GitHub hosts the source, documentation, and downloadable builds.

OpenSpace and Gemini are planned integrations, not completed features. A separate Cloudflare NASA-image cache has been implemented and tested locally but has not been deployed or connected to the game.

Where we want to take it

Today, a child begins with a simple mission: guide solar-panel cleaning before a fictional radiation-storm deadline.

Next, we want to introduce an adaptive system with new astronauts with different strengths, limited resources, and changing missions that deepen understanding of how the systems connect.

Tomorrow, that child could be the one making these calls on Mars.

Made with love by Team Roshan Xingbo at the NASA Space App Hackathon 2026, NYC.
